newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Spain vows to help expose truth of "Dirty War".
newsitem.headline: Spain vows to help expose truth of "Dirty War".

text.p: Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar vowed Tuesday to help relatives of hundreds of Spaniards who disappeared in Argentina's "Dirty War" in the late 1970s learn the truth about their loved ones' fate.

"Logically, Spain wants the truth to be known and the memory to live on, so that things like this do not and cannot ever happen again," Aznar told a news conference in Buenos Aires on the last day of a three-day visit.

Spain's relations with Argentina, a key trading partner, suffered tensions after a Spanish judge investigating the fate of Spanish victims of military repression recently ordered the arrest of former Argentine military ruler Leopoldo Galtieri.
Tens of thousands of people, among them up to 600 Spanish citizens, were abducted and killed by the Argentine military in a crackdown on suspected leftists in their 1976-83 regime.
Spanish Judge Baltasar Garzon is investigating the fate of 300 of them and wants Galtieri tried for allegedly ordering the deaths of three personally.

Garzon is also looking into reports that secret Argentine files detailing the circumstances of Dirty War abductions and killings were sent to Switzerland via Spain in 1983. Human rights groups want the files so that they can find out where, when and why the victims died.
Aznar said the Spanish government "has no information about files produced by previous Argentine governments."

But the Spanish leader, who met relatives of the missing on Monday, promised them legal help from the Spanish embassy to fight on in the Argentine courts and to track down the children of "the disappeared" sold into adoption by the military.

"We have also asked families for all information possible about what might be the situation of the children of the Spaniards who disappeared," Aznar said, adding however that Spain would act "with respect for Argentine law."

Argentina insists it cannot extradite Dirty War leaders like Galtieri because they were already tried and jailed after the return of democracy in 1983, and were subsequently pardoned by President Carlos Menem in 1989.
Earlier this month, Argentine Foreign Minister Guido Di Tella accused the Spanish judge of what he called archaic and imperialist behaviour for issuing an arrest warrant for Galtieri.
